source_document.body:
One concern after another was raised by the buy side analysts who follow C.H. Robinson and RXO on the phone call that Monday morning rapidly followed the shocking announcement that C.H. Robinson, the largest broker in the U.S., was buying RXO, generally considered the 3rd biggest 3PL.
What about antitrust concerns? How will you handle technology integration? What kind of legal “docket” does RXO face?
And one by one, those concerns were swatted away. Given that most of the analyst questions included a “congratulations” to C.H. Robinson CEO Dave Bozeman, it seemed clear that Wall Street was sold on the close to $6 billion acquisition.
The shock nature of the deal was best expressed by Tom Wadewitz of UBS on the call. He noted that C.H. Robinson had “talked about being active in acquisitions, but I think this is bigger than expected.”
The two C.H. Robinson executives on the call, Bozeman and CFO Damon Lee, repeatedly said the deal was not done with the legal fallout from the Montgomery vs. Caribe Transport II case in mind. Still, the term “post Montgomery world” was kicked around during the call, and it represented more of an acknowledgement that the 3PL industry is going to change beyond just protecting itself legally.
“I do certainly think in the post-Montgomery world that the flight to quality is important,” Lee said. “So I think that factors into our confidence.” Shippers who were confident in using C.H. Robinson and RXO separately, Lee said, “are going to be even more confident in our capability as a combined entity. Post-Montgomery, this makes the discussion a lot easier as well.”
The end goal numbers are that RXO (NYSE: RXO) is being valued at approximately $5.8 billion in the deal, and that the combined company will have an enterprise value of more than $25 billion.
RXO up on Monday, down on Tuesday
The initial reaction on Wall Street to the merger Monday was a sharp increase in the price of RXO stock–not surprising given that at the very least, the cash-only option or cash portion for shareholders is $30.25 per share–and a decline in the price of C.H. Robinson.
At approximately 1:05 p.m. EDT Tuesday, C.H. Robinson (NASDAQ: CHRW) stock was down $6.63, or 4.72% to $133.98. A day earlier, C.H. Robinson was down $17.11 to $140.61, a drop of 10.85%.
The Monday increase for RXO did not carry into Tuesday. Also at about 1:05 p.m. EDT, RXO was down 37 cts, or 1.29%, to $28.28. It was closer to flat by the end of the day.
One day earlier, RXO finished up $5.27 to $28.65, a gain of 22.54%. The stock price has not reached the cash portion of the deal.
But even if investors right out of the gate may have not been fans of the deal, those sell side analysts with their congratulations told a different story.
Analysts see the synergies as doable
A focus on the post-announcement reports from investment banks was C.H. Robinson’s projections that synergies in the deal will be worth $300 million and that the deal would be accretive to earnings within nine months of the deal’s close, which is anticipated in the first half of next year. Longer-term, C.H. Robinson said the merger would be “mid-teens accretive to adjusted EPS in 2028.”
In the first half of 2026, C.H. Robinson reported adjusted EPS of $2.95, which was up 19.9% from a year earlier.
In a report that it slugged “First Read,” analysts at UBS said that “a backdrop where CHRW has been very good at realizing cost synergies and visibility to stronger truckload volume growth is limited, we believe the deal makes clear strategic sense.”
The decline in the C.H. Robinson price Monday (when the UBS report was published) “provides opportunity, but we also realize it will take time for more visibility to deal integration & other risks.”
At Bank of America Merrill Lynch, the transportation research team led by Ken Hoexter made a similar argument: the drop in the C.H. Robinson stock price, for now, makes sense. But so do the company’s arguments in favor of the deal.
Bank of America Merrill Lynch held its buy rating on the stock, but said its Price Objective was cut to $203 from $226 “as we account for equity dilution in the expected deal.”
The argument for significant cost savings is solid, the bank said. “We believe CHRW’s productivity track record sets a credible path to narrowing RXO’s productivity gap and exceeding its $300 mil synergy target,” it said in its report.
Ratings agencies check in
There was one significant mildly dissenting voice on the strengths of the deal: S&P Global Ratings.
While S&P Global (NYSE: SPGI) did not change its rating on C.H. Robinson–it would not make such a move that quickly–it did shift the outlook on its debt rating to negative.
Both S&P Global and Moody’s (NYSE: MCO) by the end of the day Monday had affirmed their current rating on C.H. Robinson, a BBB+ from S&P Global and Baa2 at Moody’s. Both are investment grade, but the S&P rating is considered higher on an equivalency scale.
In the call with analysts, Bozeman said he expects the deal would not impact the company’s investment-grade debt rating. In an interview with FreightWaves, he added that discussions with the ratings agencies took place as part of the process C.H. Robinson undertook in agreeing to acquire RXO, which is a fairly standard practice for companies about to make a big acquisition.
But S&P Global’s move to negative went one step further than Moody’s, which did not change the outlook on the company.
With new debt to be taken on to finance the acquisition, S&P Global described the expanded levels as “meaningful.”
Those levels are significant enough, S&P Global said, that it will create a need for C.H. Robinson “to materially increase S&P Global Ratings-adjusted EBITDA to achieve credit measures we view as commensurate for our rating on the company. It also reflects our view of the prolonged timing to close, and industry uncertainty in the subsequent 24 months thereafter that could impact our forecasts.”
Identifying the metrics
Among the standards S&P Global and Moody’s looks at in publishing a rating, the ratio of funds from operations (FFO) to debt is a key metric. It is one of the reasons for S&P Global’s move to a negative outlook.
The acquisition, S&P Global said, “will cause expected proforma FFO to debt at close (mid to high 20% area) to be materially below our stated downside scenario (45%), and we consider the potential for integration challenges that could preclude a sufficient and timely improvement.“ To offset that, S&P said, C.H. Robinson will need both growth in EBITDA (as measured by S&P Global, as it is not a standard definition) and “material debt repayment.”
To help strengthen the company’s finances, C.H. Robinson said it would halt stock buybacks until it reaches its “target leverage ratio.” That target, according to the company’s statement announcing the acquisition, is 1.75x to 2.25x net debt to adjusted EBITDA by the end of 2028 for the trailing 12 months.
Moody’s said in its affirmation of its C.H. Robinson debt rating that its estimate is that the 3PL’s debt-to-EBITDA ratio will be approximately 3.6x at the end of 2027, but should fall to about 2.4x by the end of 2028.
Not a lot of overlap
Once the talk on the analysts’ call got past the finances Bozeman talked about the fact that this was not going to be a merger of two companies that are essentially a mirror image of each other.
“We will have an expanded business mix with the combined company offering more solutions across the supply chain,” Bozeman said. “This network density and diversity will allow us to do enhanced freight matching, improve service levels and better compete across transportation markets.”
Both Bozeman and Lee made several references to C.H. Robinson’s “cost to serve efficiencies,” with the estimated synergy savings coming in part from taking RXO’s activities and have them operating under those efficiencies.
Lee said the amount of customer overlap is “a very de minimis number. It is not material at all.”
He said RXO “has built a fantastic business with a technology-enabled platform, a talented team with deep industry expertise, strong customer relationships, a high-quality carrier network, and a proven track record of growth.”
In its presentation to analysts, C.H. Robinson said the number of shippers it serves is 75,000. By contrast, RXO’s shipper network is 18,000.
Carriers served by C.H. Robinson total 450,000. At RXO, its pool is a third of that: 150,000.
One key distinction between the two companies is the level of activity underneath the core truck brokerage. C.H. Robinson’s North American Surface Transport (NAST) segment accounts for 73% of gross revenue. AT RXO, truck brokerage is the same amount. (The entire RXO operation at C.H. Robinson will be under NAST, which is headed at C.H. Robinson by Michael Castagnetto).
But Last Mile is 19% at RXO. Global Forwarding at C.H. Robinson is 18%. Those respective strengths that are not overlapping were viewed as a key reason supporting the deal.
Bozeman said the “complementary” last mile and transportation solutions business at RXO “are where they truly excel.”

source_document.body:
By Jim Evans - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=94231487
The US is planning a lot more gas power – and data centers are the culprit. Proposed grid-connected gas capacity has nearly tripled since early 2023, while plans for new wind power are shrinking.
A new analysis and interactive map from Environment America Research & Policy Center and Frontier Group puts the planned gas buildout at 60.4 gigawatts (GW) through the end of 2030. That’s up 44% from the 41.8 GW expected in December 2025, based on filings submitted to the federal Energy Information Administration (EIA).
For perspective, that proposed new gas capacity alone exceeds the total generating capacity of every individual US state except Texas, California, and Florida, according to the groups.
These are planned projects, so the figures don’t mean all that capacity will get built. But they show how quickly the US power industry’s plans are shifting toward gas as electricity demand climbs.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Meanwhile, planned solar additions have stalled, and planned wind additions have dropped 33.9% since December 2025. Solar still leads the list of expected new generating capacity, but the groups warn that clean energy plans aren’t keeping pace with the data center boom.
“The data is clear: Surging electricity demand to power data centers is putting our nation’s transition to clean energy at risk,” said Andre Delattre, senior vice president and chief operating officer for The Public Interest Network. “Given the lifespans of new gas plants, these facilities could lock America into decades of continued fossil fuel dependence. Any potential benefits of data centers won’t mean anything if we destroy the planet in the process.”
Texas leads the gas buildout
Texas accounts for 33.2% of the proposed new grid-connected gas capacity through 2030 – roughly a third of the national total. If built, those projects would expand the state’s existing gas generating capacity by almost 25%.
Louisiana follows with 6.6 GW, then Pennsylvania with 4.4 GW, Oklahoma with 3 GW, and Mississippi with 2.6 GW. Together, those five states account for about 60% of the planned additions.
And the tally leaves out a potentially big chunk of the picture: off-grid gas plants built to supply data centers directly. The groups say those projects could add tens of gigawatts more.
The pollution cost
Burning gas produces pollution that contributes to soot and ground-level ozone. The climate impact also extends beyond the smokestack: methane, the main ingredient in natural gas, can escape during production and transportation.
The analysis cites modeling that estimates nearly 600,000 asthma symptom cases and about 1,300 premature deaths in 2028 under a high-growth scenario for data centers. That estimate covers pollution from fossil fuel power plants, on-site gas turbines, and backup diesel generators serving data centers.
The concern is how long the consequences could last. Building gas plants to meet today’s demand could leave the US burning fossil fuels for decades.
“If we build new gas plants, in addition to delaying the retirement of coal plants and slowing the growth of renewables, we jeopardize our health, our planet, and the well-being of future generations,” said Johanna Neumann, senior director of the Campaign for 100% Renewable Energy at Environment America Research & Policy Center.

source_document.body:
( The views expressed here are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent the views of FreightWaves or its affiliates. )
As if C.H. Robinson did not have enough going on with its recent acquisition announcement with RXO , six trucking companies sued the global 3PL as well as Total Quality Logistics in Texas federal court. On September 23, Stevens Trucking, Western Flyer Express, Freymiller, IWX Motor Freight, Christenson Transportation, and E.O.S. alleged the brokers grew by handing loads to carriers that cut costs with forced labor, fake logs, and safety shortcuts. They want lost profits, treble damages, and attorneys’ fees.
And here it is. These motor carrier plaintiffs worked for a shipper & allegedly lost the business to TQL & CH. They argue they cannot service the account in a cost effective way, because the defendants allegedly use unsafe carriers. Spoiler: that’s not how RICO works pic.twitter.com/vsv6MeIuPO — Matthew Leffler (@ArmchairAtty) October 2, 2026
What a Civil RICO Case Requires
A civil RICO case lets a business sue over injuries caused by a pattern of serious federal crimes . The Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act targets ongoing criminal enterprises. To win, a plaintiff must prove four things. The defendant conducted or joined an “enterprise.” The defendant committed a “pattern” of racketeering, at least two related crimes within ten years. The enterprise affected interstate commerce. And the plaintiff lost business or property “by reason of” that violation. Wire fraud and forced labor both count as predicate crimes. Winners can collect three times their losses plus attorney fees. Here the carriers say the brokers and certain carrier networks used false electronic bids and forced labor to undercut lawful rates.
The Lost Contracts They Claim
Damages center on lost bids and squeezed margins. Stevens says Armacell and Ford graded most of its 2026 bids 20 percent or more above benchmark. IWX claims about $21 million in missed Driscoll’s linehaul revenue and later scaled back. Western Flyer reports losing nearly all direct Pilgrim’s Pride volume from a Texas plant and failing every lane in a Graphic Packaging bid. Christenson’s revenue fell about 30 percent, from $71 million in fiscal 2023 to $50 million in fiscal 2025. Freymiller lists $51 million in lost sales across 63 customers. E.O.S. points to eroded Graphic Packaging freight from the Texarkana mill. Some say they hauled as subcontractors at a loss just to keep drivers. These motor carriers want those losses tripled under RICO.
Why Anza v. Ideal Steel Matters
The Supreme Court’s 2006 ruling in Anza v. Ideal Steel Supply Corp. is the key precedent. Ideal Steel sued a rival that allegedly skipped New York sales tax on cash sales. The unpaid tax allowed the rival to charge less and steal customers. The Court said Ideal could not recover under RICO. The direct victim was the state, not the competitor. Lost sales were too indirect. Other factors could explain why buyers chose the cheaper shop. Justice Kennedy wrote that RICO needs a direct link between the illegal act and the claimed injury. A plaintiff cannot simply argue the defendant meant to grab market share.
The parallel is plain. The Plaintiff carriers say the brokers’ use of non-compliant carriers produced low bids that cost them lanes with shippers such as Graphic Packaging, Pilgrim’s Pride, Kroger, Driscoll’s, and Ford. The alleged crimes most directly harm drivers, misled shippers, and the public. The carriers’ lost contracts sit further down the chain, much like Ideal’s lost sales. Courts applying Anza often dismiss competitor RICO claims for this reason.
How the Plaintiffs Score on Roadside Inspections
At its core, this case is about allegedly dubious, unsafe motor carrier capacity in the United States. Amid unprecedented levels of public scrutiny over the business of safely delivering freight on time and undamaged, we see a far more energetic Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration focusing its efforts on this very issue. It does beg the question about the Plaintiff motor carriers own safety and maintenance records. Unfortunately, public FMCSA data for the last 24 months shows mixed records.
Driver out-of-service rates are strong and well below the national average of about 6.7 percent: Stevens roughly 1.2 percent, Western Flyer 1.1 percent, Freymiller 0.6 percent, IWX 1.1 percent, Christenson 1.5 percent, and E.O.S. 1.3 percent. Vehicle-maintenance out-of-service rates (national average about 22 percent) vary. IWX is near 8 percent and Freymiller near 18 percent, both better than average. Stevens, Western Flyer, and Christenson run in the mid-to-high 20s. E.O.S. is higher still, around 33 percent. The numbers do not prove the complaint, but they show the plaintiffs may not be free of maintenance issues even while driver compliance looks solid.
What Happens Next
I expect an early motion to dismiss built on Anza . If the court finds the injuries too remote, the RICO counts may fall. False-advertising claims could remain though. Discovery into broker files and shipper bids would be slow and costly. A settlement is possible if the brokers want to limit scrutiny of their carrier networks, but the causation hurdle is high. That said, this suit may serve as a roadmap to bring similar suits against other large 3PLs. Whether the case survives will turn less on how unsafe the disputed carriers may be and more on whether lost bids by rival trucking companies are the kind of direct injury RICO was written to cover.
Matthew Leffler is a transportation attorney, adjunct professor of law at Michigan State University College of Law, and the host of the Armchair Attorney® Podcast. He can be reached at matthew@armchairattorney.com

source_document.body:
Fusion energy company Xcimer Energy said it has finalized an agreement for up to $30.5 million in additional federal funding through the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE’s) Milestone-Based Fusion Development Program .
The new DOE award, announced October 6, is for the program’s second budget period. It brings the total DOE funding for potential Milestone payments to Xcimer to $39.5 million as part of the federally supported fusion energy development program. Xcimer, headquartered in Denver, Colorado, in 2024 received a $4-million award from the government’s ARPA-E agency for a total of $43.5M in non-dilutive federal funding.
Energy Secretary Chris Wright (second from left) toured Xcimer Energy’s Denver facility in December 2025. Source: Xcimer Energy
“America invented laser fusion, and America should lead its commercialization,” said Dario Gil, the DOE’s Under Secretary for Science. Gil, who leads the federal government’s Genesis Mission project, delivered a keynote address in late September at POWER’s Experience POWER event in Washington, D.C. “The Milestone-Based Fusion Development Program is built to turn American scientific leadership into commercial capability by putting private capital and private-sector execution behind ambitious, measurable goals. Xcimer is making real progress toward a new generation of laser fusion technology, and this award will help accelerate that work.”
Excimer Laser Architecture
Xcimer is developing an excimer laser architecture designed specifically for the requirements of a commercial fusion power plant. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on large numbers of solid-state laser beams and expensive optical components, Xcimer’s architecture uses cost-effective gas lasers, durable gas optics and a two-beamline configuration designed to deliver megajoule-scale laser energy repeatedly and economically, according to the company.
This is a rendering of Xcimer Energy’s proposed Athena power plant architecture. The U.S. Dept. of Energy has approved the plant’s design. Source: Xcimer Energy
“We have moved from proving that the physics works to building the industrial technology that can turn fusion into a commercial energy source,” said Conner Galloway, co-founder and CEO of Xcimer Energy. “This additional milestone funding gives us another powerful mechanism to accelerate that work while keeping the majority of the investment and risk in the private sector. We are building the laser, manufacturing systems and supply chain required to make commercial laser fusion possible.”
Xcimer’s commercial fusion program is targeting electricity on the grid in the mid-2030s.
Phoenix Laser System
Xcimer in June of this year launched operations of Phoenix, the world’s largest privately owned laser system, which demonstrates key elements of Xcimer’s excimer-laser and gas-optics architecture. Phoenix is housed in Xcimer’s 74,000-square-foot Denver laser facility. POWER toured the lab on June 4. The company calls Phoenix “a proof of concept for an unconventional fusion architecture: a krypton fluoride [KrF] excimer laser using Stimulated Brillouin Scattering [SBS] to compress a microsecond-long pulse into the nanosecond timescales fusion requires. Phoenix is designed to demonstrate end-to-end integrated operation of excimer amplification and SBS pulse compression.”
This is a view from inside Xcimer Energy’s Phoenix laser facility in Denver, Colorado. Source: Xcimer Energy / Photo by Edward DeCroce Xci.
The DOE this past summer approved the preconceptual design and technology roadmap milestones for Xcimer’s commercial power-plant architecture, Athena, also part of the DOE’s Milestone Program.
Xcimer and RTX in September announced a partnership to develop directed-energy air defense systems based on Xcimer’s pulsed laser technology. The companies plan to demonstrate the integration and containerization of Xcimer’s pulsed lasers with RTX’s air defense systems, offering the U.S. military new capabilities to defeat airborne threats. RTX also invested in Xcimer, directly strengthening Xcimer’s laser fusion energy roadmap.
Xcimer Energy is developing powerful lasers for commercial fusion energy and national security. The company has raised about $200 million from leading investors. including Breakthrough Energy Ventures, founded by Bill Gates; Lowercarbon Capital, Emerson Collective, Prelude Ventures, and others.
— Darrell Proctor is a senior editor for POWER.

Transfix has integrated driver identity verification from E3 Group into its transportation management system (TMS), giving freight brokers a way to screen drivers for fraud before releasing a pickup number.
The integration brings E3’s driver authentication tools into the Transfix TMS rather than requiring brokers to move between separate systems to verify a driver’s identity, according to the companies’ Oct. 6 announcement .
The technology checks driver credentials, truck information and other risk signals before a load is picked up. Transfix said brokers can see the results within the shipment workflow and keep a record of the verification with the load.
The integration comes as freight fraud increasingly involves deceptive pickups, in which criminals use fake identities, forged credentials and carrier impersonation to obtain legitimate loads. Overhaul recorded 574 cargo theft incidents in the U.S. during the first quarter of 2026 and said deceptive pickup schemes increased 31% year over year. Highway , meanwhile, found that communication-based attacks, including compromised inboxes, spoofed emails, account takeovers and impersonation calls, accounted for 50% of classified freight-fraud vectors in the second quarter, up from 42.7% in the first quarter.
Transfix’s move follows similar integrations by other transportation software providers. In June, Transfix integrated Highway’s carrier identity and compliance technology into its TMS, allowing brokers to conduct carrier verification and fraud checks without leaving the platform. In July, AscendTMS integrated SearchCarriers’ carrier intelligence into its built-in verification system, giving users access to carrier and broker risk data within the TMS.
How the verification works
Transfix’s integration with E3 is specifically aimed at the point where a driver is assigned to a load. E3’s system verifies the driver’s identity against information including a commercial driver’s license, truck and carrier records, while also examining device, location and contact information.
E3 says its system analyzes more than 50 signals, including biometric data, and uses biometric matching and liveness detection to verify that the person presenting the credentials is the driver associated with the load. E3 says its system can review more than 60 fraud signals on each load.
Drivers consent to photo capture and temporary location capture on the first page of E3’s verification form, according to the company. E3 said it deletes personally identifiable information after it is no longer needed for essential use, in compliance with privacy laws.
The verification is completed through a web page rather than a mobile app. If authentication fails, E3 withholds the pickup number and alerts the broker or compliance team, with the brokerage making the final decision on whether to move forward.
Transfix said the integration can prevent a pickup number from being released until the driver’s authentication is completed.
“The check happens at dispatch and not in a report someone reads a week later,” Jonathan Salama, co-founder and CEO of Transfix, said in the announcement.
Direct Traffic Solutions is among the first brokers using the integration. The company said it did not need a separate integration project or additional vendor login to use E3 through Transfix.
E3 said it could not provide load-level results specific to Direct Traffic Solutions. However, the company said that across its customer network, it has authenticated drivers on more than 650,000 loads and is currently reviewing about 5,000 drivers per day. E3 said its customers have recorded zero stolen loads to date.
Zooming out
Driver verification addressed one part of the cargo-theft problem: making sure the person arriving to collect a load is actually the driver and truck associated with the shipment.
The focus on driver-level verification comes as theft groups use legitimate carrier identities and fraudulent communications to gain access to freight. CargoNet said theft by deception groups are expected to continue focusing on shipments tendered to legitimate carriers, potentially sidestepping compliance controls that have traditionally centered on the tendering process itself.
For brokers, the integration could reduce the number of manual checks required before a load moves, while giving them a record of the verification process inside the same system used to manage the shipment.
Why this matters
Driver impersonation and deceptive pickups are becoming a bigger part of freight fraud, making carrier-level verification alone less effective. Transfix’s integration with E3 moves identity checks into the TMS workflow, allowing brokers to verify the driver before releasing pickup information and adding another layer of protection against fraudulent pickups.

The E-Space Concept is an all-electric reboot of Renault’s iconic minivan from the 1980’s.
Renault brings back the E-Space as an EV
Renault is bringing the minivan back, but this time as a fully electric people mover. With the futuristic E-Space Concept, Renault said it’s “rebooting the spirit” of the original Espace that launched in 1984.
While Renault already sells the Espace as an SUV , this one will be closer to the iconic MPV from the ’80s.
Renault said the “E” in E-Space refers to its E-Tech, or “Electrified Technology,” if you will. Meanwhile, “Space,” as you might guess, refers to the spacious, high-tech interior.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Measuring 4,700 mm long, Renault’s electric minivan is about the same size as the Kia PV5 and Volkswagen ID. Buzz SWB, which it will directly compete against.
The concept retains a similar design to the first Espace, but with a modern twist. It features a wide “U”-shaped light strip at the front and rear, plus an illuminated floating diamond pattern at the front center. The square running lights look nearly identical to the Renault 5.
First-generation Renault Espace MPV I (Source: Renault)
Renault has yet to reveal specifics, but the company is moving to introduce lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries across its entire EV lineup to lower costs, so the electric minivan will likely follow suit.
According to Auto Express , the minivan will use Renault’s new RGEV Medium 2.0 platform, which could deliver a driving range of around 500 miles. The platform also supports an extended-range electric vehicle (EREV) configuration.
Renault Espace III (Source: Renault)
We will learn more when Renault unveils the E-Space Concept on October 12 at the Paris Motor Show.
Renault will showcase three concept cars, including the E-Space, the Renault 8 Gordini Concept, and the Renault 4 JP4x4 Concept.
New models, including the Megane E-Tech Electric, Trafic E-Tech Electric, a “hyper-customized” version of the Renault 5 Turbo 3E, and the special-edition Rafale Hypnotic, will also be on display.

source_document.body:
Toyota’s joint venture, FAW Toyota, issued a statement denying reports that it’s “slashing prices” in China and may exit the market entirely.
Toyota denies false reports of price cuts in China
Toyota sells vehicles in China through two joint ventures: FAW Toyota and GAC Toyota. The long-standing joint ventures produce and sell Toyota models, including the Corolla, RAV4, and Avalon, as well as new electric vehicles like the bZ3 and bZ5.
Last week, on September 28, GAC Group announced plans to acquire a 50% stake in FAW Toyota. The plans include issuing new A-shares priced at 5.75 yuan per share.
Under the agreement, GAC said that FAW Group would become its second-largest shareholder, but exact details would be finalized following an audit and once the valuation work was complete.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
FAW Toyota was established in 2000 as a joint venture between FAW Group and Toyota, with each holding a 50% share. It was initially called Tianjin FAW Toyota Motor Co until 2003, when it adopted the name FAW Toyota.
Toyota bZ5 (Source: Toyota)
Once the agreement is finalized, GAC Group would take FAW’s 50% stake, while Toyota would retain the other 50%. GAC said the deal would not change the controller.
The move was widely viewed as part of Toyota’s efforts to revamp slumping brand sales in China and streamline operations.
Toyota bZ3 (Source: Toyota)
Since the announcement, several reports have claimed that FAW Toyota plans to exit the market completely and is slashing prices to sell down inventory.
FAW Toyota issued a statement on Monday night, refuting the false claims. The company said:
In response to false statements circulating on certain online platforms —such as claims that “FAW Toyota may completely exit the market” and “Toyota is slashing prices”—our company reserves the right to pursue legal action.
The joint venture added that “the production, sales, and iterative development plans for all models are progressing smoothly as scheduled.”
Looking ahead, FAW Toyota will leverage the Group’s broader resources and technology for upcoming vehicles.
Toyota’s sales in China fell by 22.8% in August, marking the seventh straight month of lower sales due to weak demand for gas and hybrid models amid soaring fuel prices.

reference.quote: Anduril Industries plans to invest $3.7 billion in a submarine-component manufacturing facility at Tradepoint Atlantic , the multimodal logistics development at the Port of Baltimore .

context_references.quote: Anduril Industries plans to invest $3.7 billion in a submarine-component manufacturing facility at Tradepoint Atlantic , the multimodal logistics development at the Port of Baltimore .

source_document.body:
Anduril Industries plans to invest $3.7 billion in a submarine-component manufacturing facility at Tradepoint Atlantic , the multimodal logistics development at the Port of Baltimore .
The plant would create 3,100 permanent jobs and return shipbuilding to the former Bethlehem Steel property at Sparrows Point. The 2 million-square-foot facility is expected to begin initial operations in 2030.
The Arsenal-2 project will manufacture components for the U.S. Navy’s Virginia-class nuclear-powered attack submarines to be shipped to Huntington Ingalls (NYSE: HII ) in Newport , Va., and General Dynamics (NYSE: GD )Electric Boat in Groton, Ct., for final assembly.
Anduril initially expects to produce smaller components, including torpedo tubes, before expanding into larger submarine sections such as bows and sterns.
The Navy has awarded Anduril a $2.9 billion contract, according to a company announcement. President Donald Trump was scheduled to visit Tradepoint Atlantic on Oct. 6 to promote the project.
The contract is controversial, having been awarded just days after Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey was appointed along with Elon Musk and former Republican Congressman Newt Gingrich to a Pentagon weapons advisory group. It also comes weeks ahead of the midterm elections where incumbent Democratic Gov. Wes Moore is on the ballot, along with eight seats in the House of Representatives.
Maryland officials told local media the development is the state’s largest single private investment and its largest job-creation project in more than a decade. The project is expected to support more than 14,000 total jobs, including the permanent positions at the facility, according to a Maryland Department of Commerce announcement. Anduril estimates it will generate more than $2 billion in annual economic output and about $312 million in annual wages.
“With this facility, thousands of Marylanders will have new pathways to work, wages and wealth through advanced training and high-skilled maritime manufacturing jobs,” Gov. Wes Moore said in the announcement.
Return to shipbuilding
The facility will occupy the general area of the former Bethlehem Steel shipyard, reconnecting Sparrows Point with the maritime manufacturing activity that once helped define the site. Tradepoint Atlantic acquired the property in 2014 and has since redeveloped it into a logistics hub with warehouses, distribution centers and marine operations.
Mediterranean Shipping Co., the world’s largest container line, broke ground earlier this year for a new $1.2-billion box terminal at the site.
Public incentives require approval
Maryland and Baltimore County have committed to matching up to 13% of Anduril’s anticipated private investment through existing incentive programs and new appropriations. Portions of that support will require approval from the Maryland General Assembly and Baltimore County Council.
Baltimore County’s proposed contribution includes a personal property tax incentive worth up to $210 million over 30 years, WYPR reported.
The state package also includes capital support for a workforce-training center. Maryland plans to seek a federal Maritime Prosperity Zone designation for the region.
Port and rail access
Tradepoint Atlantic’s deepwater port, rail and highway connections, and access to a large regional workforce helped attract the investment, officials said. Anduril also cited the East Coast location’s proximity to other submarine contractors as a factor in selecting Maryland after considering sites elsewhere in the country.
The 3,300-acre logistics and industrial complex is part of the Port of Baltimore. Its marine terminal and private railroad provide waterfront access, commodity storage and connections to both CSX (NASDAQ: CSX ) and Norfolk Southern (NYSE: NSC )
Anduril has signed a long-term lease at Tradepoint Atlantic, although the company has not disclosed its duration. The manufacturing operation is expected to expand in the years following its planned 2030 opening.

reference.quote: Transportation prices surge as capacity tightens further in September

context_references.quote: Transportation prices surge as capacity tightens further in September

source_document.body:
Old Dominion Freight Line was named the top national less-than-truckload carrier for a 17th straight year while Daylight Transport received top overall honors for a third straight year, according to a news release from Mastio & Co. The research and consulting firm annually conducts the industry’s most comprehensive survey evaluating customer value and loyalty.
This year’s results were based on 1,647 telephone interviews with LTL shippers from June through September. Respondents provided approximately 5,300 evaluations, rating 155 carriers, with 24 earning ratings sufficient to make the report.
Key decision makers were asked open-ended questions about carrier service offerings, competitiveness and customer retention. The rankings are historically based on 28 service metrics, including on-time delivery, damages, transit times, pricing and technology, as well as back-end functions like billing accuracy, claims processing, problem resolution and carrier responsiveness.
Thomasville, North Carolina-based Old Dominion ( NASDAQ: ODFL ) said it ranked No. 1 in 24 of the evaluated service categories, “including carrier trustworthiness, ease of doing business, timely customer service, and shipments delivered when promised.”
“This award is very important to us because it is selected by shippers,” said Marty Freeman, president and CEO of Old Dominion, in a Tuesday news release. “They count on OD to do more than just move their freight – we are an extension of their brand and true business partners.”
Two other national carriers—privately held Estes and publicly traded XPO ( NYSE: XPO )—also exceeded the industry benchmark for national operators.
Richmond, Virginia-based Estes was named best value provider among national carriers for a fifth consecutive year. It also received the top ranking for competitive pricing and website usefulness. The carrier, like others, has been actively increasing its door count to enhance its service offering.
“These results offer a meaningful perspective on how shippers experience Estes — from the value they receive to the people and tools they interact with every day,” the company said in a statement. “We’re proud of this feedback and will continue to listen, improve, and find new ways to make the shipping experience even better for the people we serve.”
Greenwich, Connecticut-based XPO recorded the largest year-over-year increase in net promoter score and weighted performance score among all national carriers. The carrier’s recent quarterly earnings report validated these improvements.
Cypress, California-based Daylight Transport was also named the top inter-regional carrier in addition to top overall honors.
Repeat regional winners included: Pitt Ohio (Northeast/Mid-Atlantic), Dayton Freight Lines (Great Lakes/Midwest) and Peninsula (Western). Averitt Express was the overall winner in the Southern region.
Why it matters? Mastio’s annual survey provides a comprehensive, data-backed benchmark of carrier performance across key service metrics like on-time delivery and pricing. Additionally, it highlights market leaders and direct shipper feedback, giving companies valuable insight into the service standards and customer expectations that drive carrier selection.

reference.quote: Shadow EW represents a critical shift in how we think and how BAE Systems develops and delivers our products, specifically the cost-effective electronic warfare that is highly manufacturable, in order to scale and get these to our warfighter in a rapid manner.

context_references.quote: Shadow EW represents a critical shift in how we think and how BAE Systems develops and delivers our products, specifically the cost-effective electronic warfare that is highly manufacturable, in order to scale and get these to our warfighter in a rapid manner.

source_document.body:
presented by
BAE Systems’ Shadow EW™ compact electronic warfare (EW) solutions provide critical situational awareness and self-defense capabilities for a diverse and growing range of small airborne platforms. (BAE Systems)
If there’s one request of electronic warfare (EW), it’s that it can be disruptive from farther distances yet still compact for small airborne platforms, drones, and mass munitions at the aerial layer that are presently dominating ground conflicts around the world.
To bring greater offensive EW capability to the aerial layer, BAE Systems has introduced its small-form-factor software defined radio (SDR) family of products. Shadow EW brings greater offensive capability to modern and legacy aerial systems. Breaking Defense spoke with Dan Mooney, director of business development, and Rebecca Cruz, director, Shadow EW products, at BAE Systems, about how Shadow EW brings new benefits to smaller platforms.
Breaking Defense: Electronic warfare is changing rapidly. What is the threat scenario driving the need for smaller, more efficient SDRs?
Mooney: The No. 1 thing that we see, the demand from our customers, is increased range. The main things that are changing are longer range systems, smaller systems, and access into the increased areas of denial.
Dan Mooney, director of business development, BAE Systems
With that, the need for scalability in EW systems to enable area access for these small on-demand, or medium- or large-class platforms, that’s really the need that we see, is to increase the range of unmanned systems and entry into highly contested environments to our war fighters’ systems.
How is EW evolving?
Mooney: The key here is the timelines. What is required today is a shorter response time in terms of the rapidly evolving EW environment. Things that used to take either years or months to adapt to now require a timeline of days, or a matter of hours.
We’re able to leverage software as the key enabler so that we can meet the mission of the day. Making sure that the war fighter has these systems available to them when they need it – that is the goal of Shadow EW. It’s the ability to upgrade to things like software, firmware, not a hardware material type change. It’s a software change so that these systems are available when needed.
Rebecca Cruz, director, Shadow EW products, BAE Systems
Cruz: The Shadow EW systems are not designed to be bespoke products for any singular platform. They’re designed to support rapid payload insertion and meet a number of different needs across varying mission sets.
What are the specific EW capabilities that you’re looking at for platforms such as drones or mass munitions? How does that vary from a larger, more traditional platform?
Mooney: They don’t necessarily vary much. The Shadow EW system is developed and targeted to address affordable mass systems, but can also scale to things like higher-speed type systems or things like an exquisite-type platform in the unmanned realm. What we’re focused on here isn’t necessarily any reduction or addition of capabilities, it’s a reduction of SWaP (size, weight and power) and enabling those key features to be available to these lower-cost, unmanned or attritable systems.
Cruz: The modularity is critical here, too. With the system being modular as it is, you can purchase different boxes, including the SDR, to place on a platform instead of just one large exquisite system.
Mooney: The beauty of Shadow EW are the capabilities, or jobs, that used to take two, three or four boxes now is hosted within a singular system at a reasonable price point for the platform to lower the logistical implementation of multiple boxes, smaller SWaP and a lower price point of an all-in-one system.
What capabilities do these systems offer compared to legacy systems?
Mooney: The keys here are situational awareness, targeting, survivability, deception, and collaborative behavior. These are all things that as our customers look for network collaborative autonomy and behaviors, being able to leverage those across things like targeting, survivability and deception, we’re able to do that across these unmanned systems.
How quickly is Shadow EW able to adapt to new threats?
Mooney: I can’t get into all the details and specifics of that, but with Shadow EW, we’re able to partner with the warfighter to be able to meet their timelines given the mission. I can tell you with certainty that it’s not months or years. We are working on the timelines that the warfighter dictates to us, and as a partner with them to be able to meet the mission of the day and not be the squeaky wheel.
Cruz: That drives to our commercial stance. Part of the reasoning for driving to commerciality is we heard the Department of War talk about getting things fielded into the warfighter’s hands quicker. BAE Systems has and is continuing to internally invest to get apps built, to get hardware built, so that we have things readily available to field quicker to the warfighter.
As products get old, we are working through refresh cycles. We’re continuing to refresh that software, firmware and stay ahead of emerging threats so that when new threats emerge, we have more options to provide to our customers.
Your systems are software-defined; what about the hardware?
Mooney: Beyond just the software piece, it’s the agnostic nature of the hardware, as well. We’re not bespoke to any certain apertures and antennas, not bespoke against any singular interface or standard, it’s open standards. Software is the key, but as new platforms come online, we want that rapid insertion. The Shadow EW systems are not bespoke to the other parts of the RF radio frequency package.
Cruz: As a part of that product refresh cycle, we are closely tuned in and tied in with our business development teams and such that we’re consistently monitoring the needs, the warfighters’ needs, the market, and working to stay ahead of any changes that need to be made to that architecture. As we refresh the products, we’re being informed by the communications that our business development teams are bringing back to us.
What should be the takeaways about Shadow?
Cruz: The environment is changing, as Dan said, sometimes even by the minute. Shadow EW represents a critical shift in how we think and how BAE Systems develops and delivers our products, specifically the cost-effective electronic warfare that is highly manufacturable, in order to scale and get these to our warfighter in a rapid manner.
The product delivers a big punch in a small box, and they are meant to address that low-cost need that our warfighters have been looking for and asking for to protect our nation and protect themselves in their day-to-day operations.
Mooney: Shadow enables access to the best of breed for what BAE Systems does. With our history and our pedigree with electronic warfare, it’s commonplace to think of delivering these large systems that are quite expensive. Whereas here, as Rebecca said, highly manufacturable, high volume, and able to be lower cost to meet budgets of respective programs.
It also enables access for customers with Shadow EW to proven capabilities from BAE Systems’ EW prowess. Capabilities that have been proven in simulation environments, in operational theater, Shadow EW leverages down into a smaller box at a lower SWaP available when needed. Don’t think tens or hundreds of systems, think multiple thousands.
